claim: Chen et al. reported evidence for inter-nucleus recombination in arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi in 2018.
source: Chen et al. recently reported evidence for inter-nucleus recombination in arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (Chen et al., 2018a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018a

claim: After filtering the data by excluding heterozygous sites in haploid nuclei, duplicated regions of the genome, and low-coverage depths base calls, the evidence for recombination is very sparse.
source: After filtering the data by excluding heterozygous sites in haploid nuclei, duplicated regions of the genome, and low-coverage depths base calls, we find the evidence for recombination to be very sparse.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1 and Table 1

claim: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi were presumed to be asexual for many years because no one had witnessed sexual structures in these fungi.
source: For many years arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) were presumed to be asexual as no one had witnessed sexual structures in these fungi.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge about historical understanding of AMF

claim: AMF retain core meiosis genes.
source: AMF retain core meiosis genes (Halary et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Halary et al., 2011

claim: A meiosis-like process most likely occurs in the AMF lineage.
source: AMF retain core meiosis genes (Halary et al., 2011), indicating that a meiosis-like process most likely occurs in this lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of core meiosis genes

claim: Previous evidence for recombination in AMF was based on duplicated gene copies.
source: Previous evidence for recombination later turned out to be based on duplicated gene copies (Croll and Sanders, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Croll and Sanders, 2009

claim: Previous evidence for recombination in AMF was based on ribosomal RNA sequences that were paralogs.
source: Previous evidence for recombination later turned out to be based on duplicated gene copies (Croll and Sanders, 2009), or ribosomal RNA sequences that were paralogs (Pawlowska and Taylor, 2004; Maeda et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pawlowska and Taylor, 2004 and Maeda et al., 2018

claim: The isolates studied by Chen et al. were dikaryotic, containing nuclei of two classes defined by their mating type (MAT) locus.
source: The isolates were dikaryotic, containing nuclei of two classes defined by their mating type (MAT) locus (Ropars et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ropars et al., 2016

claim: Applying each filter individually removed between 19–77% of recombined positions.
source: Applying each filter individually removed between 19–77% of recombined positions.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Figure 1

claim: Filtering of low coverage sites had the strongest effect, a ~75% reduction in recombined positions.
source: Filtering of low coverage sites had the strongest effect, a ~ 75% reduction.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Figure 1

claim: Applying all three filters together removed 91% of recombined sites.
source: Applying all three filters together removed 91% of recombined sites (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Figure 1

claim: The combined application of all three filters reduced the total number of sites by only ~22%.
source: Notably, these filters had much less effect on the total number of analyzed sites, with the combined application of all three filters reducing the total number of sites by only ~22%.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Figure 1

claim: After filtering, no consecutive SNPs remained for strain A4.
source: After filtering no consecutive SNPs remained for strain A4.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Table 1

claim: Filtering applied to strains A5 and SL1 reduced the number of recombined blocks to 2 and 4, respectively.
source: Filtering applied to strains A5 and SL1 reduced the number of recombined blocks to 2 and 4, respectively
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Table 1

claim: Filtering reduced the length of the remaining recombined blocks in strains A5 and SL1.
source: Filtering applied to strains A5 and SL1 reduced the number of recombined blocks to 2 and 4, respectively, and also reduced the length of the remaining blocks.
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Table 1

claim: Chen et al. filtered out multi-copy sites if BLAST results returned more than two good hits, but retained regions with two BLAST hits.
source: The filtering used in Chen et al. (2018a) removed multi-copy sites '[i]f BLAST results returned more than two good hits', but retained regions with two BLAST hits.
evidence: Describes the methodology used in Chen et al., 2018a

claim: Retaining regions with two BLAST hits could lead to the inclusion of SNPs that are heterozygous due to duplicated regions of the genome.
source: This could lead to the inclusion of SNPs that are heterozygous due to duplicated regions of the genome.
evidence: Logical inference about the consequences of the filtering method

claim: Several positions on scaffold 70 from isolate A4 were heterozygous in several nuclei.
source: We found that several positions on scaffold 70 from isolate A4 were heterozygous in several nuclei (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by the reanalysis data presented in Figure 2

claim: High sequencing depth (>30) eliminates rare sequencing errors as the cause of heterozygosity.
source: High sequencing depth (>30) eliminates rare sequencing errors as the cause.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sequencing error rates and coverage depth

claim: A BLAST search against the A4 reference genome with sequences from scaffold 70:100354–100657 resulted in two BLAST matches: the self match on scaffold 70 and an additional match on scaffold 3570.
source: To test if duplicated regions could be the cause of the heterozygosity, we performed a BLAST search against the A4 reference genome with sequences from scaffold 70:100354–100657. This search resulted in two BLAST matches: the self match on scaffold 70, as well as an additional match on scaffold 3570 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by the BLAST analysis data presented in Figure 2B

claim: When the short reads of the dikaryon were aligned to the reference genome, both the SNPs on scaffold 70 and their match on scaffold 3570 were heterozygous.
source: When the short reads of the dikaryon (bulk sequencing of all nuclei) were aligned to the reference genome, both these SNPs on scaffold 70 and their match on scaffold 3570 were heterozygous
evidence: Supported by the alignment data presented in Figure 2B

claim: The BLAST hit result for both scaffold 70 and scaffold 3570 showed 100% identity match.
source: the BLAST hit result for both showed 100% identity match.
evidence: Supported by the BLAST analysis data

claim: The repeated sequence on scaffolds 70 and 3570 seems to have been assembled as a chimera of the two variants in both scaffolds.
source: Thus, this repeated sequence seems to have been assembled as a chimera of the two variants in both scaffolds
evidence: Inferred from the BLAST and alignment data

claim: Short reads from either copy of the repeated sequence are mapped equally to both scaffold 70 and scaffold 3570.
source: the short reads from either copy are mapped equally to both.
evidence: Inferred from the alignment data showing heterozygosity at the same positions

claim: Repetitive regions need to be excluded from analyses of recombination.
source: We feel this example illustrates the need to exclude repetitive regions from analyses of recombination.
evidence: Inferred from the example of duplicated regions causing false signals

claim: The data presented in Chen et al. was filtered with a minimum of two reads.
source: The data presented in Chen et al. (2018a) was filtered with a minimum of two reads.
evidence: Describes the methodology used in Chen et al., 2018a

claim: A minimum of two reads is a very low threshold and insufficient even for a consensus in the event of disagreeing reads.
source: This is a very low threshold, and insufficient even for a consensus in the event of disagreeing reads.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sequencing coverage requirements

claim: SL1 nuclei had ~95% fewer high coverage sites (average of 97 sites > 10 read depth) compared to A4 and A5 (2290 for A4 and 2441 for A5).
source: Looking at the distribution of read depths, overall SL1 nuclei had ~95% fewer high coverage sites (average of 97 sites > 10 read depth for nuclei from SL1 versus 2290 for A4 and 2441 for A5) compared to A4 and A5 (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by the coverage analysis data presented in Figure 3

claim: SL1 nuclei cover much less of the genome (14%) compared to A4 and A5 (53% and 42%, respectively).
source: We note here, as described in Table 1 of Chen et al. (2018a), that SL1 nuclei cover much less of the genome (14%) compared to A4 and A5 (53% and 42%, respectively).
evidence: Supported by data from Table 1 of Chen et al., 2018a

claim: For A4 and A5, recombined sites are overrepresented by sites with low depth compared to sub-sampled non-recombined sites.
source: Another fact visible from Figure 3 is that, for A4 and A5, recombined sites are overrepresented by sites with low depth compared to sub-sampled non-recombined sites (Wilcoxon ranked sum test A4; p=3.2×10−09, A5 p=2.9×10−6).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the coverage data presented in Figure 3

claim: For nuclei from isolate SL1, fewer overall recombined sites can be identified since the decreased breadth of coverage reduces overlap between nuclei.
source: We note that for nuclei from isolate SL1, fewer overall recombined sites can be identified since the decreased breadth of coverage reduces overlap between nuclei
evidence: Logical inference from the low coverage breadth of SL1 nuclei

claim: After applying filters, almost all differences between nuclei of one mating type disappear in A4 and A5.
source: After applying our filters, we find that in A4 and A5 almost all differences between nuclei of one mating type disappear (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by the pairwise SNP analysis data presented in Figure 4

claim: For nuclei from SL1, the filtering reduced the differences within a mating type, but the overall dataset is reduced such that on average nuclei only share 9 SNPs that can be compared.
source: For nuclei from SL1, the filtering reduced the differences within a mating type, but since these nuclei cover so little of the genome, the overall dataset is reduced such that on average nuclei only share 9 SNPs that can be compared.
evidence: Supported by the pairwise SNP analysis data presented in Figure 4

claim: Many nuclei from SL1 have no overlapping SNPs and no comparison can be made.
source: Many nuclei have no overlapping SNPs and no comparison can be made (black squares in Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by the pairwise SNP analysis data presented in Figure 4

claim: A few nuclei of opposite mating types, such as nuclei 17 and 25, show high similarity, but for these pairs the similarity is based on only one or two shared SNP positions.
source: A few nuclei of opposite mating types, such as nuclei 17 and 25, show high similarity, but for these pairs the similarity is based on only one or two shared SNP positions.
evidence: Supported by the pairwise SNP analysis data presented in Figure 4

claim: Nucleus 07 of SL1 shows a strong similarity with nuclei of the alternate mating type, seen by the clustering of nucleus 07 with MAT-5.
source: In Figure 2 of Chen et al. (2018a), nucleus 07 of SL1 shows a strong similarity with nuclei of the alternate mating type, seen by the clustering of nucleus 07 with MAT-5.
evidence: Describes results from Chen et al., 2018a

claim: Nucleus 07 was PCR-genotyped to be of mating type MAT-1.
source: However, this nucleus was PCR-genotyped to be of mating type MAT-1.
evidence: Describes results from Chen et al., 2018a

claim: The incongruence between PCR-genotyped mating type and the SNP clustering would be evidence of recombination spanning the MAT locus.
source: The incongruence between PCR-genotyped mating type and the SNP clustering would be evidence of recombination spanning the MAT locus.
evidence: Logical inference about what the incongruence would indicate

claim: There were no Illumina sequencing reads of nucleus 07 mapped to either mating type locus.
source: We found that there were no Illumina sequencing reads of nucleus 07 mapped to either mating type locus
evidence: Supported by the mating loci mapping analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The whole genome amplification step may not have amplified the mating locus for nucleus 07.
source: indicating the whole genome amplification step may not have amplified the mating locus.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of Illumina reads mapping to the mating locus

claim: There is no available evidence for the mating type of nucleus 07.
source: As such, we have no available evidence for the mating type of this nucleus.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of Illumina reads mapping to the mating locus

claim: Without corresponding Illumina evidence, the PCR product represents the only remaining evidence for recombination after read filtering.
source: Without corresponding Illumina evidence, we consider the PCR product the sole remaining evidence of this recombination event. This PCR experiment that is not confirmed with Illumina data represents the only remaining evidence for recombination after read filtering.
evidence: Inferred from the filtering results and lack of Illumina confirmation

claim: Cross-contamination of the PCR is a more likely scenario than recombination in the face of many billions of sequenced bases from an Illumina run.
source: We find cross-contamination of the PCR to be a more likely scenario in the face of many billions of sequenced bases from an Illumina run.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about the most likely explanation

claim: Removing low coverage sites, repeated regions, and heterozygous sites from haploid data is commonplace in genomic analyses.
source: We do not consider our filters to be particularly strict, as removing low coverage sites, repeated regions, and heterozygous sites from haploid data is commonplace in genomic analyses.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about standard genomic analysis practices

claim: In SL1, three blocks of consecutive SNPs remained after filtering.
source: In SL1, three blocks of consecutive SNPs remained after our filtering
evidence: Supported by the filtering analysis data presented in Table 1

claim: In A5, two regions of consecutive SNPs remained after filtering.
source: In SL1, three blocks of consecutive SNPs remained after our filtering, and two regions in A5.
evidence: Supported by the filtering analysis data presented in Table 1

claim: Some regions likely remain after filtering because the heterozygosity filter requires a minimum of ten reads, thus low coverage heterozygous sites are not excluded.
source: Some of these regions likely remain because our heterozygosity filter requires a minimum of ten reads, thus low coverage heterozygous sites are not excluded.
evidence: Logical inference about why some regions remain after filtering

claim: The analysis used the first 100 contigs, covering approximately 10 Mb.
source: This analysis used the first 100 contigs, covering approximately 10 Mb.
evidence: Describes the scope of the reanalysis

claim: Finding only a handful of putative recombined SNPs cannot be confidently separated from amplification/sequencing noise.
source: As such, finding only a handful of putative recombined SNPs certainly cannot be confidently separated from amplification/sequencing noise.
evidence: Inference based on the small number of remaining recombined sites

claim: Small blocks of genetic exchange may be compatible with gene conversion.
source: While small blocks of genetic exchange may be compatible with gene conversion
evidence: Based on established knowledge about gene conversion

claim: The limited number of markers involved greatly increases the difficulty in identifying high-confidence gene conversion events.
source: the limited number of markers involved greatly increases the difficulty in identifying high-confidence gene conversion events (Wijnker et al., 2013; Qi et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wijnker et al., 2013 and Qi et al., 2014

claim: Mapping recombination inside repetitive regions would require longer reads than available from standard short-read technologies.
source: Mapping recombination inside repetitive regions would require longer reads than available from standard short-read technologies.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about sequencing technology limitations

claim: Mapping recombination inside repetitive regions has been accomplished using linked short reads from individual pollen cells.
source: This is a formidable task due to the input requirements of PacBio technologies, but it has been accomplished using linked short reads from individual pollen cells (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sun et al., 2019

claim: The use of a more contiguous reference genome will actually include additional repetitive regions.
source: Notably, the use of a more contiguous reference genome will actually include additional repetitive regions
evidence: Based on established knowledge about genome assembly and repetitive regions

claim: The exclusion of repetitive regions will become even more important with a more contiguous genome assembly.
source: the use of a more contiguous reference genome will actually include additional repetitive regions, and the exclusion of repetitive regions will become even more important.
evidence: Logical inference from the fact that more contiguous assemblies include more repetitive regions

claim: A more contiguous genome assembly would not change the analysis because the apparent recombined blocks are much smaller than the contigs.
source: As the apparent recombined blocks are much smaller than the contigs, a more contiguous genome assembly would not change our analysis.
evidence: Logical inference based on the size of recombined blocks relative to contigs

claim: Single nucleus genome amplification with multiple displacement amplification produces extremely variable genome coverage.
source: Single nucleus genome amplification with multiple displacement amplification produces extremely variable genome coverage.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about multiple displacement amplification

claim: Normalization of the data was shown to improve the quality of AMF genomic data when coverage is variable.
source: Normalization of the data was shown to improve the quality of AMF genomic data when coverage is variable (Montoliu-Nerin et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Montoliu-Nerin et al., 2019

claim: Low coverage sites could still be used with a model-based approach, which incorporates the associated uncertainty.
source: In addition to normalization, low coverage sites could still be used with a model-based approach, which incorporates the associated uncertainty (Hinch et al., 2019; Bloom et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hinch et al., 2019 and Bloom et al., 2013

claim: Removing heterozygous sites from haploid single-nuclei seems like a self-evident requirement.
source: Finally, removing heterozygous sites from haploid single-nuclei seems like a self-evident requirement.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about haploid data analysis

claim: The conserved meiosis genes found in the genomes of Glomeromycotan species strongly suggests a meiosis-like process allowing recombination and re-shuffling of genetic material among genomes.
source: The conserved meiosis genes found in the genomes of Glomeromycotan species strongly suggests a meiosis-like process allowing recombination and re-shuffling of genetic material among genomes.
evidence: Inference based on the presence of conserved meiosis genes

claim: Uncovering the details of the meiosis-like process in Glomeromycota would be a major scientific breakthrough.
source: Uncovering the details of this process would be a major scientific breakthrough.
evidence: Speculative statement about the significance of the research

claim: Claims made regarding recombination in Glomeromycota require rigorous examination.
source: Given this importance, claims made regarding recombination in Glomeromycota require rigorous examination.
evidence: Inference based on the importance of the research question

claim: The models presented in Chen et al. are valuable framework to test hypotheses for meiosis-like mechanisms found in these fungi.
source: While we acknowledge that the models presented in Chen et al. (2018a) are valuable framework to test hypotheses for meiosis-like mechanisms found in these fungi
evidence: Evaluative statement about the models in Chen et al., 2018a

claim: The data presented in Chen et al. are not robust enough to support or reject the models for meiosis-like mechanisms.
source: the data presented are not robust enough to support or reject them.
evidence: Inference based on the reanalysis results

claim: One of the greatest remaining mysteries in mycology remains unknown.
source: As such, we believe that one of the greatest remaining mysteries in mycology remains unknown.
evidence: Speculative statement about the state of knowledge in mycology
